title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
abstract: Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables. Code, data and scripts to reproduce all experiments: https://github.com/anapaulaappel/QPUScheduler

bite.hook: A new scheduler predicts QPU success in milliseconds, outperforming standard compilation-based selection.
tldr: The author developed a training-free estimator that predicts QPU success probability without needing to compile the circuit.
The scheduler uses this estimate to filter candidate QPUs before committing to a full compilation process.
The method reduces latency by 25x and achieves a 0.95 Spearman correlation with actual hardware success rates.
bite.whyItMatters: As quantum computing moves to multi-vendor clusters, efficiently matching circuits to the right hardware is critical for avoiding failed jobs and wasted time.
bite.eli5: Imagine you have a bunch of different computers to run a complex task. Instead of trying to run the task on every single one to see which works best, this tool 'guesses' which computer will succeed in milliseconds, saving huge amounts of time.
